item.problem_title: Positivity diagnostics describe weights instead of naming which patient histories are unsupported
item.problem_statement: A deterministic treatment strategy can assign a treatment that clinicians almost never give to patients with certain covariate histories. The standard response is to inspect the weight distribution and truncate the tail. Truncation is bias-variance regularization: it cannot identify an effect where the treatment density is structurally zero, and a marginal weight summary does not say which intervention-relevant histories carry small or zero density. What a reader needs and does not get is a policy-specific support criterion fixed in advance, diagnostics localized by time and by history, the fraction of the target population that fails the criterion, and the estimand that survives once those strata are set aside. Empirically, poor overlap has been shown to defeat adjustment methods that were otherwise well specified, which is the failure a weight histogram is least able to show. Software

Clone-censor-weight and sequential emulation handle the misalignment; neither chooses the grace period or the interval width, and estimates move with both. A coarse interval lets treatment affect an outcome inside the interval before censoring applies; a fine interval produces high-dimensional nuisance models and unstable weights. item.paper: Quantification of the healthy worker effect: a nationwide cohort study among electricians in Denmark.
item.evidence: The design supplies a working negative-control procedure: an occupation with no known harmful exposure is used so that any nonzero rate ratio is bias, and three reference groups calibrate its magnitude, yielding 0.60 against the general population versus 1.01 (0.87 to 1.19) against the construction industry. That converts residual confounding into a measured quantity. It does not close the entry: the negative control is not paired with a proxy or validation dataset, no threshold declares the residual bias acceptable, and nothing in the reporting standard requires such a control.

item.problem_title: Transporting an observational estimate compounds sampling assumptions on top of confounding assumptions with no accounting
item.problem_statement: An internally valid estimate need not apply to the health system, population or calendar period where the decision will be made. Transporting an observational contrast requires treatment exchangeability in the source, effect exchangeability across samples conditional on a sufficient measured set, and positivity for both treatment and sampling. A sufficient set is weaker than every effect modifier: modifiers that do not differ across populations or that are irrelevant after conditioning need not be observed. Transport estimators are now being applied to emulations, including post hoc standardization of emulations to their trial populations inside a benchmarking program. What remains is the accounting. item.paper: Testing and estimating model-adjusted effect-measure modification using marginal structural models and complex survey data.
item.evidence: A concrete procedure is supplied for stacking a sampling assumption on a confounding assumption: the analysis weight is the product of the survey weight and an inverse-probability-of-exposure weight, and the second must itself be estimated using the first, with code given. It does not close the entry: the uncertainty from the two layers is not separated, the interval is only known to be conservative rather than correct, and no sensitivity analysis probes the sampling model the way the confounding model is probed.

item.evidence: The positivity requirement is translated from a statement about weights into an explicit list of histories that must be populated: for the two-point binary example it names the four covariate-treatment strata that must contain subjects following the regime, and it establishes that no support is needed among people who already deviated. verdicts.reason: The paper directly identifies why nuisance-model cross-validation under a generic prediction loss need not optimize causal-estimator performance and develops a parameter-targeted alternative. That addresses an important portion of the problem, but it does not yield a default longitudinal selection rule jointly controlling balance, weight tails, and remainder behavior.

item.problem_title: Cross-validation for longitudinal nuisance models optimizes prediction, not causal performance
item.problem_statement: Identifying a sustained-strategy effect requires consistency, sequential exchangeability and positivity, and the estimator families differ in which nuisance components they need. When those components are fitted by machine learning, the model that predicts treatment best is not the model that minimizes the finite-sample error of the causal estimator: a highly adaptive learner can achieve excellent discrimination while returning near-zero treatment probabilities, poor longitudinal balance and invalid inference. Balance-calibrated weight fitting exists and has been applied, so the field is not selecting on prediction alone. What is missing is a criterion that combines predictive risk with the estimator-specific diagnostics that matter, longitudinal balance, weight tails and the remainder-rate condition, in one selection rule, and a default library tuned that way rather than for prediction.
item.paper: Targeted maximum likelihood based causal inference: Part I.
item.evidence: The mismatch is named exactly: cross-validation optimizes a global loss-specific dissimilarity while the variance of the causal parameter is of smaller order than the variance of the nuisance fit, so an optimally cross-validated fit of the longitudinal factors yields an overly biased substitution estimator. A concrete replacement is supplied, the square of the efficient influence curve as a targeted loss whose cross-validated risk equals the asymptotic variance of the resulting estimator. It does not close the entry: that loss is evaluated at the true treatment mechanism, so the criterion is exact only where the mechanism is known, and Part I contains no simulation or data showing how much a prediction-optimal fit loses against a targeted one.
item.quote: This is due to the fact that cross-validation makes optimal choices w.r.t. the (global) loss-function specific dissimilarity, but the variance of Ψ(Qn ) is of smaller order than the variance of Qn itself.
